### The Hour Without Witnesses

At 4:17 in the morning, the city belongs to people who are not trying to be seen.

In a bakery below street level, a man in a flour-dusted apron slides the first loaves into the oven. The window is dark. No one is there to admire the pale scoring on the crusts or the practiced turn of his wrist. He works with the radio off, listening to the small ticks of the building as it warms.

A night bus crosses the nearly empty avenues. Its driver slows at stops where no one waits, because the timetable, like a promise, does not depend on being believed. There is one passenger near the back, asleep against the glass, holding a paper bag on her lap as carefully as if it contained a sleeping bird.

In a hospital, a nurse writes the time on a chart and resists the urge to round it off. On a sixth-floor balcony, a man waters a plant he is almost certain has died. He does it anyway. Hope is not always a feeling. Sometimes it is a small, repeated embarrassment.

We like to imagine the world as a sequence of events: arrivals, departures, discoveries, catastrophes. But most of the world is maintenance. Most of it is someone tightening a screw before it comes loose, replacing a worn cable, checking a lock, skimming the foam from a pot, noticing that a friend has gone quiet.

These acts rarely become stories. They leave no dramatic wreckage, no triumphant photograph. Their success looks exactly like nothing happening.

By the canal, the water is the color of old pewter. A heron stands beneath a bridge, so still it might be an abandoned piece of machinery. Then it folds itself upward, slowly at first, and rises with a few immense strokes of its wings. For a moment the surface keeps the disturbance of its going. Rings travel outward, touch the stone bank, and return changed.

Soon the sky begins to pale. Not dramatically; dawn is seldom as theatrical as we remember it. The blackness simply becomes less certain. Rooflines appear. A traffic light changes for an empty intersection. Somewhere, an alarm goes off and is silenced with the intimacy of long practice.

The first commuters will see only a wet street, a lit bus, a loaf of bread waiting behind glass. They will not see the hour that prepared these things. They will not need to.

The baker will go home as others are leaving theirs. The nurse will step outside and find the morning air strangely cold. The man on the balcony will notice, or imagine he notices, a fleck of green at the base of the dead plant.

And the city will begin again, standing as all days do on the shoulders of things almost no one saw.
